etymology: English Nonconformist minister and hymn writer (1674-1748), called the "Father of English Hymnody."
biblical_def: Isaac Watts was an English Nonconformist minister, theologian, and poet, justly called the Father of English Hymnody for transforming the worship-song of the English-speaking church. In his day congregations sang only metrical psalms, often laboriously; Watts argued that the church should sing not merely the words of the Old Covenant but the praises of Christ revealed in the New, and so he composed hymns of "human composure" that gave voice to the gospel. From his pen came some of the greatest hymns in the language: When I Survey the Wondrous Cross, that matchless meditation on the crucified Savior; Joy to the World, his paraphrase of Psalm 98 fitted to the coming of Christ; O God, Our Help in Ages Past, from Psalm 90; and Alas! and Did My Saviour Bleed. His Psalms of David Imitated recast the Psalter in the light of the gospel, "in the language of the New Testament." Watts wedded sound doctrine to singable verse, that the truths of grace might dwell richly in the hearts of ordinary believers. He stands in the dictionary as the father of English hymnody, who taught the church to sing the gospel, and whose hymns still carry the doctrine of the cross into the mouths and hearts of the people of God.

corruption_summary: Watts's legacy honors the recovery of doctrinally rich congregational song, against a modern worship that often trades the substance of the gospel for shallow sentiment and repetition.
corruption_paragraphs: Substance-for-sentiment correction. Much modern worship-song has thinned to vague feeling and endless repetition, emptied of the doctrine that once filled the church's praise. Watts shows a better way: his hymns are dense with the gospel — the cross, the sovereignty of God, the hope of glory — set to memorable verse. The dictionary holds that the word of Christ is to dwell in us richly as we sing (Col 3:16); the church's song is a vehicle of doctrine, and to strip it of truth is to impoverish the people of God.

This entry faces little postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is singing the gospel itself. Watts insisted that the church should sing not merely the shadows of the Old Covenant but the revealed glory of Christ. The dictionary commends his conviction: Christian praise should be full of Christ crucified and risen, that in singing the saints might preach the gospel to one another and glory in nothing save the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ (Gal 6:14).

etymology: English minister and hymn writer (1725-1807), former slave-trader converted by grace, author of Amazing Grace.
biblical_def: John Newton was an English clergyman and hymn writer whose own life became a living parable of the sovereign grace he sang. As a young man he was a profane and rebellious sailor and then a slave-trader, sunk in wickedness, until the mercy of God arrested him — famously during a violent storm at sea — and brought him through a long pilgrimage to faith in Christ. Ordained late in life, he became a beloved pastor at Olney and London, and with his friend William Cowper produced the Olney Hymns. From his pen came Amazing Grace, the hymn of a wretch saved by grace that once was lost and now is found; Glorious Things of Thee Are Spoken; and How Sweet the Name of Jesus Sounds. To the end he marveled at his rescue, writing as his own epitaph that he was "a servant of slaves in Africa, was, by the rich mercy of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ, preserved, restored, pardoned." In age he confessed, "my memory is nearly gone; but I remember two things: that I am a great sinner, and that Christ is a great Saviour." Newton stands in the dictionary as the trophy of amazing grace, who taught the church to sing of the mercy that saves the chief of sinners.
webster_summary: English minister and hymn writer (1725-1807), a former slave-trader saved by grace; author of Amazing Grace and the Olney Hymns, whose life became a living parable of God's mercy to the chief of sinners.

corruption_summary: Newton's life honors the recovery of grace as truly amazing — sovereign, unmerited, reaching the worst of sinners — against a sentimental religion that has tamed grace into mere niceness and lost the wonder of salvation.
corruption_paragraphs: Grace-tamed correction. The word "grace" has been softened in modern speech into mere kindness or tolerance, losing its biblical weight. Newton's life recovers the wonder: grace is the sovereign mercy that reaches a blaspheming slave-trader, the chief of sinners, and makes him a servant of Christ. The dictionary holds that grace is unmerited favor shown to the ill-deserving (Eph 2:8); to feel its true force one must first see the depth of sin from which it saves, as Newton never ceased to do.

This entry faces little postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the wonder of personal salvation. Newton never got over his own rescue; "Amazing Grace" is the song of a man astonished to the end that mercy found him. The dictionary commends his example against a casual, presumptuous religion: the saved sinner ought to marvel that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom — with Paul and Newton — he is chief (1 Tim 1:15).

etymology: English poet and hymn writer (1731-1800), friend of John Newton and co-author of the Olney Hymns.
biblical_def: William Cowper was one of the foremost English poets of his age and a hymn writer of rare tenderness, the close friend and Olney neighbor of John Newton, with whom he produced the Olney Hymns. His faith was real and his gifts great, yet his life was shadowed by recurring seasons of severe melancholy and despair, in which he sometimes doubted his own salvation; and out of that crucible came hymns of profound comfort for the afflicted soul. From his pen came God Moves in a Mysterious Way, that great hymn of trust in providence amid darkness; There Is a Fountain Filled with Blood, on the cleansing power of Christ's atonement; and O for a Closer Walk with God. Newton's steady friendship was a means of grace to Cowper in his darkest hours. Cowper's life is a moving testimony that genuine faith may coexist with deep suffering of mind, and that the believer who walks in darkness may yet trust in the name of the LORD (Isa 50:10). He stands in the dictionary as the poet of providence in the shadows, who taught the church that God hides a smiling face behind a frowning providence, and that the fountain of Christ's blood cleanses even the most despairing sinner.

corruption_summary: Cowper's life honors the recovery of trust in God's providence amid darkness and the reality that true believers may suffer deep affliction of mind, against a shallow religion that equates faith with constant cheerfulness.
corruption_paragraphs: Health-and-happiness correction. A shallow religion teaches that genuine faith always feels happy and that the suffering of the mind betrays unbelief. Cowper's life refutes the lie: here was a true believer who walked through long seasons of crushing melancholy, and yet wrote hymns of deep faith. The dictionary holds that the people of God may walk in darkness and have no light, and are called there to trust in the name of the LORD and stay upon their God (Isa 50:10); affliction of soul is not proof of lost faith.

This entry faces little postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is trust in the inscrutable providence of God. Cowper sang that God "moves in a mysterious way His wonders to perform," hiding "a smiling face" behind "a frowning providence." The dictionary commends this faith for the afflicted: the believer cannot always trace God's hand, but he may trust His heart, for the unsearchable judgments of God (Rom 11:33) are always wise and always good, even in the dark.

etymology: English clergyman and hymn writer (1740-1778), staunch Calvinist, author of Rock of Ages.
biblical_def: Augustus Montague Toplady was an English clergyman, a convinced and vigorous Calvinist, and the author of one of the best-loved hymns in the language, Rock of Ages, Cleft for Me. Converted as a youth under the preaching of a lay Methodist, he came to embrace the doctrines of sovereign grace with fervent conviction, and he contended earnestly — sometimes sharply — against the Arminian theology of John Wesley, defending the absolute freeness and efficacy of God's saving grace. His great hymn distills the heart of the gospel: the sinner has nothing to bring and must hide wholly in the cleft Rock, Christ crucified — "Nothing in my hand I bring, simply to thy cross I cling." It is a hymn of pure grace, casting the soul entirely upon the finished work of Christ for both pardon and cleansing. Toplady wrote other hymns and doctrinal works defending Reformed truth, and died young, at thirty-seven, rejoicing in the assurance of his salvation. He stands in the dictionary as the singer of Rock of Ages and a defender of sovereign grace, who taught the church that the sinner's only refuge is to cling empty-handed to the crucified Christ, the Rock cleft for the guilty.
webster_summary: English clergyman and hymn writer (1740-1778), a staunch Calvinist; author of Rock of Ages, Cleft for Me, the hymn of the empty-handed sinner casting himself wholly on the crucified Christ.

corruption_summary: Toplady's hymn defends salvation by grace alone through the finished work of Christ, against every scheme that would let the sinner bring some work or worth of his own to add to the cross.
corruption_paragraphs: Works-added correction. The perennial temptation is to bring something of our own to the cross — some merit, effort, or worth that contributes to salvation. Toplady's hymn slams the door: "Nothing in my hand I bring, simply to thy cross I cling." The dictionary holds salvation by grace alone, not of works, lest any man should boast (Eph 2:9); the sinner is saved not by works of righteousness which he has done, but according to God's mercy (Titus 3:5), clinging empty-handed to Christ.

This entry faces little postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Christ as the only refuge. Toplady draws on the Rock cleft for Moses and the spiritual Rock that was Christ (1 Cor 10:4): the guilty soul finds shelter from the wrath of God only by hiding in the wounded Savior. The dictionary commends this single hope: there is no other rock, no other refuge, no other cleansing for sin, than the crucified Christ to whom the sinner must wholly cling.

etymology: English Nonconformist minister and hymn writer (1702-1751), author of The Rise and Progress of Religion in the Soul.
biblical_def: Philip Doddridge was an English Nonconformist minister, educator, and hymn writer, one of the most influential figures of eighteenth-century Dissent. He led an academy that trained ministers, combining sound learning with warm evangelical piety, and his devotional classic The Rise and Progress of Religion in the Soul traced the work of grace from awakening through conversion to growth and assurance, becoming a means of conversion to many — including, famously, the young William Wilberforce. As a hymn writer he often composed verses to be sung after his sermons, crystallizing their message; from him come O Happy Day, That Fixed My Choice, on the joy of covenanting with Christ; Hark, the Glad Sound! the Saviour Comes; and Grace! 'Tis a Charming Sound. Doddridge united in himself the scholar, the pastor, and the poet, laboring always for the conversion of sinners and the building up of saints. He died at forty-eight, seeking health in Lisbon. He stands in the dictionary as a pastor-hymnist of the evangelical revival, who traced the rise and progress of true religion in the soul, and whose hymns gave the church glad voice to the joy of choosing Christ and the charm of His grace.
webster_summary: English Nonconformist minister, educator, and hymn writer (1702-1751); author of The Rise and Progress of Religion in the Soul and of O Happy Day, That Fixed My Choice, who traced the work of grace from awakening to assurance.

corruption_summary: Doddridge's work honors the recovery of vital, experiential religion that rises and progresses by grace, against both a dead formalism and a one-moment religion that knows nothing of growth in grace.
corruption_paragraphs: Formalism correction. Mere outward religion, learned by rote and never felt in the heart, was as much a danger in Doddridge's day as ours. His Rise and Progress traced the living work of grace in the soul, from first awakening to settled assurance, calling the formalist to a real and experiential faith. The dictionary holds that true religion is a work of God begun and carried on in the heart (Phil 1:6), not a mere outward conformity, and commends Doddridge's searching account of vital godliness.

This entry faces little postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is growth in grace. Doddridge charted not only the soul's awakening but its progress, against a shallow religion content with a single decision and no further pursuit of holiness. The dictionary commends his vision: the believer is called to grow in grace and in the knowledge of Christ (2 Pet 3:18), and the work God begins He will carry on to the day of Jesus Christ.

etymology: English Baptist hymn writer (1717-1778), the first major English woman hymnwriter, who wrote under the name "Theodosia."
biblical_def: Anne Steele was an English Baptist poet and hymn writer, widely regarded as the first significant woman hymnwriter in the English language, who published under the name "Theodosia." The daughter of a Baptist pastor and timber merchant, she lived a life marked by long affliction — chronic illness and personal sorrow, including the loss of her betrothed before their marriage — and out of that suffering came hymns of remarkable submission, comfort, and trust in God. Her hymns, gathered in Poems on Subjects Chiefly Devotional, gave voice to the believer's confidence in God's goodness amid pain; among them is Father, Whate'er of Earthly Bliss, with its tender petition, "Give me a calm, a thankful heart, from every murmur free." She wrote also hymns on the Scriptures and the Savior, exalting the Word and the worth of Christ. Steele's quiet, suffering faithfulness opened a door for generations of women who would serve the church through sacred song. She stands in the dictionary as the first great woman of English hymnody, who turned a life of affliction into songs of submission and trust, and who taught the church to bring a calm and thankful heart, free from murmuring, to the wise and loving will of God.

corruption_summary: Steele's witness honors the recovery of submission and contentment in suffering and the rightful place of godly women in the church's praise, against both a religion that cannot suffer well and a confusion of biblical womanhood.
corruption_paragraphs: Suffering-resented correction. The natural heart murmurs against affliction and demands relief. Anne Steele, through a life of pain and loss, learned to pray for "a calm, a thankful heart, from every murmur free," submitting to the wise will of God. The dictionary holds with Job, "the LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD" (Job 1:21); the believer is called not to resent suffering but to receive it from a Father's hand and find comfort in His Word (Psa 119:50).

This entry faces little postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the honored service of godly women in the church. Steele served not by seizing the pastoral office, which Scripture reserves to qualified men, but by the gift of sacred song that has fed the whole church for centuries. The dictionary commends her example: within the good order God has appointed, women have rich and vital ministries, and the church is poorer wherever the faithful labors of its godly women go unrecognized.

etymology: Scottish-born hymn writer and editor (1771-1854), son of Moravian missionaries, author of Angels from the Realms of Glory.
biblical_def: James Montgomery was a hymn writer, poet, and newspaper editor, born in Scotland to Moravian missionary parents who died on the mission field while he was young. A man of strong evangelical and humanitarian conviction, he twice went to prison for his outspoken journalism in the cause of justice, and labored for the abolition of slavery and the relief of the oppressed. As a hymn writer he gave the church some of its most enduring songs: Angels from the Realms of Glory, the great Christmas hymn summoning all creation to worship the newborn King; Hail to the Lord's Anointed, a majestic setting of Psalm 72 on the reign of the Messiah; Prayer Is the Soul's Sincere Desire, a beloved meditation on the nature of prayer; and In the Hour of Trial. His hymns combine doctrinal richness with poetic grace and a warm missionary and kingdom-minded spirit. Montgomery stands in the dictionary as a hymn writer of the Messiah's kingdom, who summoned the church to worship Christ the King and to long for the spread of His righteous reign, and who taught the people of God that prayer is the soul's sincere desire, uttered or unexpressed.

corruption_summary: Montgomery's hymns honor the recovery of the Messiah's universal reign and the true nature of prayer, against a faith that has lost the vision of Christ's kingdom and reduced prayer to mere words.
corruption_paragraphs: Kingdom-shrunk correction. A privatized, this-worldly religion loses the grand vision of the Messiah's reign over all the earth. Montgomery's Hail to the Lord's Anointed, set to Psalm 72, sings of the King whose dominion stretches from sea to sea, before whom all kings shall fall down and all nations serve. The dictionary holds the biblical hope of Christ's universal and righteous reign, and commends Montgomery's summons to long and labor for the spread of His kingdom to the ends of the earth.

This entry faces little postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the inward reality of prayer. Montgomery defined prayer as "the soul's sincere desire, uttered or unexpressed," teaching that true prayer is not mere recited words but the genuine longing of the heart toward God. The dictionary commends this against a formalism that mistakes the saying of prayers for praying: the Spirit Himself helps our infirmities, making intercession with groanings that cannot be uttered (Rom 8:26).

etymology: Scottish minister and hymn writer (1808-1889), "prince of Scottish hymn writers," brother of Andrew Bonar.
biblical_def: Horatius Bonar was a Scottish minister of the Free Church and the foremost hymn writer Scotland has produced, the brother of the saintly Andrew Bonar. A faithful pastor and a man of warm evangelical and Reformed conviction, he wrote hymns of unusual depth and tenderness that set the gospel of free grace to memorable verse. From his pen came I Heard the Voice of Jesus Say, that beloved hymn of Christ's invitation and the soul's rest in coming to Him; Not What My Hands Have Done, a clear and moving confession that salvation rests not on the sinner's works but on the finished work of Christ; and Blessing and Honour and Glory and Power. Bonar's hymns are rich with the doctrines of grace, the sufficiency of Christ, and the hope of His return, written to be sung by ordinary believers. He also wrote devotional and doctrinal works and labored for the conversion of sinners throughout his long ministry. Bonar stands in the dictionary as the prince of Scottish hymn writers, who taught the church to sing the rest that Christ alone gives and the salvation that rests not on what our hands have done but wholly on the Savior.

scriptures: Matt 11:28
Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.
John 1:29
The next day John seeth Jesus coming unto him, and saith, Behold the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sin of the world.
Gal 2:16
Knowing that a man is not justified by the works of the law, but by the faith of Jesus Christ, ... for by the works of the law shall no flesh be justified.
Rev 5:13
Blessing, and honour, and glory, and power, be unto him that sitteth upon the throne, and unto the Lamb for ever and ever.
corruption_summary: Bonar's hymns defend justification by Christ's finished work and the rest He alone gives, against every gospel that would rest salvation on the sinner's own doing or deny the soul its rest in Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: Works-rest correction. The anxious heart seeks rest in its own performance and finds none. Bonar's Not What My Hands Have Done answers plainly: "Not what my hands have done can save my guilty soul... thy work alone, O Christ, can ease this weight of sin." The dictionary holds justification by faith in Christ apart from the works of the law (Gal 2:16); the soul's rest is found not in what we have done but in what Christ has finished, and to that finished work the believer looks for peace.

This entry faces little postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the rest Christ gives. Bonar sang the gracious invitation, "Come unto me... and I will give you rest" (Matt 11:28), and the soul's answer in coming to the Savior. The dictionary commends this against a restless, striving religion: Christ bids the labouring and heavy-laden come to Him, and gives a rest the world cannot give and cannot take away, the rest of sins forgiven and a soul at peace with God.

etymology: English hymn writer (1836-1879), known as the "consecration poet," author of Take My Life and Let It Be.
biblical_def: Frances Ridley Havergal was an English hymn writer and devotional poet, often called the "consecration poet" for the theme that runs through her best-loved hymns: the glad and total surrender of the whole life to Christ. A woman of deep personal piety, exceptional memory of Scripture, and frail health, she wrote hymns that have called generations of believers to wholehearted devotion. Chief among them is Take My Life, and Let It Be Consecrated, Lord, to Thee, which offers to God in turn the believer's hands, feet, voice, lips, silver and gold, will, heart, and self — a hymn she wrote after a night of rejoicing over the conversion of others, and whose own words she took with such seriousness that she later sent away her jewelry to be sold for missions. She also wrote Like a River Glorious, on the perfect peace of trusting God, and Who Is on the Lord's Side? Havergal stands in the dictionary as the poet of consecration, who taught the church that the only reasonable response to redeeming grace is the offering of the whole life to God, holding back nothing from the Savior who gave Himself wholly for us.
webster_summary: English hymn writer (1836-1879), the "consecration poet"; author of Take My Life and Let It Be and Like a River Glorious, who called the church to the glad and total surrender of life to Christ.

scriptures: Rom 12:1
I beseech you therefore, brethren, by the mercies of God, that ye present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable unto God, which is your reasonable service.
Gal 2:20

I am crucified with Christ: nevertheless I live; yet not I, but Christ liveth in me: and the life which I now live in the flesh I live by the faith of the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself for me.
Isa 26:3
Thou wilt keep him in perfect peace, whose mind is stayed on thee: because he trusteth in thee.
And that he died for all, that they which live should not henceforth live unto themselves, but unto him which died for them, and rose again.
corruption_summary: Havergal's hymns honor the recovery of wholehearted consecration to Christ, against a half-hearted religion that would receive His grace while withholding the life He bought.
corruption_paragraphs: Half-hearted-devotion correction. It is the perennial temptation to accept the gift of salvation while reserving large portions of life from the Giver. Havergal's Take My Life refuses the reservation, offering to God hands, voice, will, heart, and self, holding nothing back. The dictionary holds that the mercies of God call for the presenting of the whole body as a living sacrifice (Rom 12:1); grace received demands a life surrendered, and to keep back parts of ourselves from Christ is to forget the price He paid.

This entry faces little postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the redeemed no longer live unto themselves. Christ died that those who live should live unto Him who died and rose for them (2 Cor 5:15). Havergal not only sang consecration but lived it, parting with her treasures for the gospel's sake. The dictionary commends her example: true faith works itself out in a life laid wholly on the altar, glad to belong entirely to the Savior who gave Himself entirely for us.

etymology: English Congregationalist author, editor, and hymn writer (1789-1855), author of 'Tis Not That I Did Choose Thee.
biblical_def: Josiah Conder was an English Congregationalist author, editor, and hymn writer, a leading literary figure of Nonconformity in his day. An editor of journals and a writer on many subjects, he was also a gifted hymn writer who compiled an important hymnbook for the Congregational churches and contributed many of his own compositions. His hymns are marked by doctrinal clarity and devotional warmth. Among the best known is 'Tis Not That I Did Choose Thee, a hymn that sets forth the priority of God's electing love: "'Tis not that I did choose thee, for, Lord, that could not be; this heart would still refuse thee, hadst thou not chosen me" — a clear confession that the sinner loves God only because God first loved him. He also wrote The Lord Is King! Lift Up Thy Voice, exalting the reign of God over all the earth, and Bread of Heaven, on Thee We Feed, a communion hymn. Conder stands in the dictionary as a hymn writer of sovereign grace, who taught the church to sing that our love for God springs not from our choosing Him but from His prior, electing love, and that the King of heaven reigns over all.
webster_summary: English Congregationalist author, editor, and hymn writer (1789-1855); author of 'Tis Not That I Did Choose Thee, the hymn of God's electing love, and The Lord Is King!

1 John 4:19
We love him, because he first loved us.
Eph 1:4
According as he hath chosen us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and without blame before him in love:
Deut 7:7
The LORD did not set his love upon you, nor choose you, because ye were more in number than any people; for ye were the fewest of all people:
corruption_summary: Conder's hymn defends the priority of God's electing love, against the man-centered assumption that our salvation begins with our choice of God rather than His choice of us.
corruption_paragraphs: Man-first correction. The natural assumption is that we come to God by our own initiative, that our choice of Him is the first cause of our salvation. Conder's hymn reverses it: "this heart would still refuse thee, hadst thou not chosen me." The dictionary holds the Savior's own word, "Ye have not chosen me, but I have chosen you" (John 15:16), and the apostle's, "We love him, because he first loved us" (1 John 4:19). Our love for God is the fruit of His prior, electing love, not its cause.

This entry faces little postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the foundation of assurance in God's electing love. If our salvation began with our choosing, it would rest on a frail and changeable foundation; because it begins with God's choosing us in Christ before the foundation of the world (Eph 1:4), it is sure. The dictionary commends Conder's hymn as both humbling and comforting: humbling, because we contributed nothing; comforting, because what God began in eternity He will surely complete.
